(Sūrat al-Munāfiqūn)
Eleven verses, Medinan

﷽

﴿When the hypocrites come to you, they say, "We testify that you are indeed the Messenger of God." God knows that you are His Messenger, and God testifies that the hypocrites are indeed liars.﴾

﷽

﴿When the hypocrites come to you, they say, "We testify that you are indeed the Messenger of God." God knows that you are His Messenger, and God testifies that the hypocrites are indeed liars.﴾

The connection of this sūrah with what precedes it is that the previous sūrah contains mention of the sending of the Messenger (ﷺ), and mention of those who denied him in heart and tongue, by way of a parable, as He said: ﴿The likeness of those who were entrusted with the Torah﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 5]. This sūrah contains mention of those who denied him in heart without the tongue, and affirmed him with the tongue without the heart. As for the first being linked to the last, it is that at the end of the previous sūrah there is an admonition to the people of faith (īmān) to honor the Messenger (ﷺ) and to observe his right after the call to the Friday prayer, and to give priority to following him in worship over others, and that abandoning honor and following him is among the traits of the hypocrites. The hypocrites are the liars, as He said at the beginning of this sūrah: ﴿When the hypocrites come to you﴾, meaning ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, ﴿they say, "We testify that you are indeed the Messenger of God."﴾ The report about them is complete, then He begins anew and says: ﴿God knows that you are His Messenger﴾, that is, He sent you, so He knows that you are His Messenger. ﴿And God testifies﴾ that they concealed other than what they displayed. This indicates that the reality of faith lies in the heart, and that the reality of every statement is likewise: whoever reports something while believing the opposite is a liar, because lying, in terms of its being a contradiction, lies between the verbal existence and the mental existence, just as ignorance, in terms of its being a contradiction, lies between the mental existence and the external existence. Do you not see that they used to say with their tongues, "We testify that you are indeed the Messenger of God," and God named them liars because their speech contradicted their belief? Some people said: God did not call them liars for their words, ﴿We testify that you are indeed the Messenger of God﴾; rather He called them liars for other falsehoods issuing from them, as in His saying: ﴿They swear by God that they did not say [it]﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74], and ﴿They swear by God that they are indeed of you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 56]. The answer to "when" (idhā) is ﴿they say, "We testify"﴾, meaning:

[Page 13]

that when they come to you they bear witness to you of the prophethood, and they are liars in that testimony, for it has already been explained that their speech contradicts their belief. In the verse there are several discussions.

The first discussion: they said, "We testify that you are indeed the Messenger of God." If they had said, "We know that you are indeed the Messenger of God," would that have conveyed the same meaning as this, or not? We say: it would not, because their saying "We testify that you are indeed the Messenger of God" is explicit in testifying to the establishment of the prophethood, whereas their saying "We know" is not explicit in establishing knowledge, since their knowledge of the unseen is with others.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield, and so they barred others from the way of God. Indeed, evil is what they have been doing.﴾ ﴿That is because they believed and then disbelieved, so a seal was set upon their hearts, and so they do not understand.﴾

His statement: ﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾, meaning, a cover by which they conceal themselves from what they feared for their own selves, namely killing. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾ may mean that their saying ﴿We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of God﴾ is one of their false oaths, since testimony (shahadah) takes the place of swearing in emphasis. A man says: 'Ashhadu and ashhadu billah' (I bear witness, and I bear witness by God), and 'a'zimu and a'zimu billah' (I resolve, and I resolve by God), in place of 'uqsimu' (I swear) and 'uli' (I swear). Abu Hanifa cited this as evidence that 'ashhadu' (I bear witness) is an oath. It may also be a description of the hypocrites in their treating oaths lightly." If it is asked: why did they say "we bear witness" and not "we bear witness by God" as you say? Some answered this by saying that it carries the sense of an oath from the believer, and in common usage it is only by God, so he reported with his saying "we bear witness" instead of his saying "by God."

His statement the Exalted: ﴿so they barred others from the way of God﴾, meaning, they turned themselves away from obedience to God the Exalted and obedience to His Messenger. It was also said: "they barred", that is, they diverted and prevented the weak from following the Messenger of God ﷺ. ﴿Indeed, evil﴾, that is, wretched is ﴿what they have been doing﴾, in that they preferred disbelief over belief and showed the opposite of what they concealed, in conformity with the Muslims.

His statement the Exalted: ﴿That is because they believed and then disbelieved﴾. "That" is a reference to His saying ﴿evil is what they have been doing﴾. Muqatil said: "That lying is because they believed outwardly, then disbelieved in secret." This contains an emphasis of His saying: ﴿And God bears witness that they are indeed liars﴾ [al-Tawbah: 107]. His statement ﴿so a seal was set upon their hearts, and so they do not understand﴾: they do not reflect, nor do they draw inferences from the manifest proofs. Ibn Abbas said: "a seal was placed upon their hearts." Muqatil said: "a seal was set upon their hearts by disbelief, so they do not understand the Qur'an and the truthfulness of Muhammad ﷺ." It was also said: they used to think that they were upon the truth, so God the Exalted informed that they do not understand that a seal had been set upon their hearts. Then there are discussions regarding the verse:

The first discussion: He, the Exalted, mentioned the deeds of the disbelievers previously and did not say "indeed, they are those who have been doing evil." So why does He say it here? We say: their deeds are linked to the false oaths which they made a shield, that is, a covering for their wealth and their blood against the Muslims' lawful seizing of them, as has passed.

The second: The hypocrites were only ever upon established, enduring disbelief, so what is the meaning of His saying the Exalted: ﴿they believed and then disbelieved﴾?

We say: Al-Zamakhshari said there are three aspects:
The first: (they believed) they uttered the statement of testimony and did what one who enters Islam does; (then they disbelieved) then their disbelief became apparent after that.

The second: (they believed) they uttered belief in the presence of the believers; (then they disbelieved) they uttered disbelief in the presence of their devils, mocking Islam, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14].

The third: that it means the people of the dhimma (protected non-Muslims) among them.

The third discussion: Setting a seal upon hearts occurs only from God the Exalted. Since God has sealed their hearts, it is not possible for them to reflect and draw inferences from the proofs. Were this so, it would be a proof for them against God the Exalted: they would say, "Our turning away from the truth is due to our heedlessness, and our heedlessness is because He, the Exalted, sealed our hearts." We say: this sealing by God the Exalted is in response to their evil deeds and their intention to turn away from the truth. It is as though He, the Exalted, left them to their own ignorance (al-jahiliyyah) and their false desires.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿When you see them, their bodies impress you; and if they speak, you listen to their speech. They are as if they were propped-up planks of wood. They think every cry is against them. They are the enemy, so beware of them. May Allah destroy them! How are they deluded?﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you," they turn their heads aside, and you see them turning away while they are arrogant.﴾ ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them; Allah will never forgive them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiant people.﴾

Know that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When you see them﴾ refers to ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy, Mughith ibn Qays and Jadd ibn Qays. They had bodies and a presence, and their bodies impress you for their goodliness and beauty. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy was tall, handsome and eloquent, and whenever he spoke, the Prophet (ﷺ) would listen to his speech. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and if they speak, you listen to their speech﴾, meaning: and they would say, "Indeed you are the Messenger of Allah," and you would listen to what they say. It was also read as yusmaʿ (passive voice). Then He likened them to propped-up planks of wood. In the word al-khushub (planks of wood) there is lightening (takhfif) as in badanah and budn, asad and usd, and heaviness (tathqil) likewise as in thamarah and thumur, khashabah and khushub, madarah and mudur. This is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas. The heavy form is the dialect of the people of al-Hijaz. Planks of wood do not understand or comprehend, and likewise the people of hypocrisy, as if in their neglect of understanding and insight they were in the position of planks of wood.

As for al-musannadah (propped-up): one says "sanada ila shayʾ," meaning he leaned towards something, and "asnadahu ila al-shayʾ," meaning he inclined it, so it is musnad. The doubling (tashdid) is for emphasis. The planks were described with it because they resemble standing trees which grow and bear fruit in some respect. Then He attributed cowardice to them and reproached them for it, saying: ﴿They think every cry is against them.﴾ Muqatil said: when a caller calls out in the army, or an animal escapes, or a lost thing is sought, for example, they think that it is aimed at them because of the terror in their hearts. That is because they are apprehensive lest Allah expose their veils and reveal their secrets, and they expect to be struck moment by moment. Then Allah informed His Messenger of their enmity, saying: ﴿They are the enemy, so beware of them﴾, that you should not trust them with secrets and should not pay attention to their outward appearance, for they are the most complete in enmity relative to others. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿May Allah destroy them! How are they deluded?﴾ is an explanation, and it is an invocation against them, and a request from Him that He curse them and humiliate them, and an instruction to the believers that they should invoke thus. ﴿How are they deluded?﴾ means: how do they turn away from the truth, in wonder at their ignorance, their error, and their corrupt assumption that they are upon the truth.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you"﴾. Al-Kalbi said: when the Qur'an descended upon the Messenger (ﷺ) describing the hypocrites, their tribesmen from among the believers came to them and said: "Woe to you! You have been exposed through hypocrisy and destroyed yourselves. Come to the Messenger of Allah, repent to him from hypocrisy, and ask him to ask forgiveness for you." But they refused that and were indifferent to seeking forgiveness, so this was revealed. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "When ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy returned from Uhud with many people, the Muslims despised him, rebuked him, and made him hear what he disliked. His own kinsmen said to him: 'If you went to the Messenger (ﷺ) so that he would ask forgiveness for you and be pleased with you.' He said: 'I will not go to him, nor do I want him to ask forgiveness for me,' and he began to turn his head, so this was revealed."

According to most, he was only called to seek forgiveness because he had said: ﴿Surely the mightier will expel the meaner therefrom﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8] and said: ﴿Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah﴾. It was said to him: "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you." He said: "What did I say?" That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they turn their heads aside﴾. It was read as lawwaw (without doubling) and with doubling, which is for multiplicity; the pronoun may be treated as plural while the intended referent is singular, and this is common in Arabic poetry. May Allah not bless those who thought you [would be] ...
except by covenant, until what happened happened.

The Mu'tazilah said: He does not name them guided when they defy and go astray. There are discussions concerning the verse:

The first discussion: why did He liken them to propped-up planks of wood and not to other useful things? We say: this comparison includes many benefits not found in others.

It may also be meant that the idols carved from wood propped against a wall: they were likened to them in the beauty of their forms and the scarcity of their usefulness.

How are they deluded?﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you," they turn their heads aside, and you see them turning away while they are arrogant.﴾ ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them; Allah will never forgive them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiant people.﴾

Know that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When you see them﴾ refers to ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy, Mughith ibn Qays and Jadd ibn Qays. They had bodies and a presence, and their bodies impress you for their goodliness and beauty. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy was tall, handsome and eloquent, and whenever he spoke, the Prophet (ﷺ) would listen to his speech. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and if they speak, you listen to their speech﴾, meaning: and they would say, "Indeed you are the Messenger of Allah," and you would listen to what they say. It was also read as yusmaʿ (passive voice). Then He likened them to propped-up planks of wood. In the word al-khushub (planks of wood) there is lightening (takhfif) as in badanah and budn, asad and usd, and heaviness (tathqil) likewise as in thamarah and thumur, khashabah and khushub, madarah and mudur. This is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas. The heavy form is the dialect of the people of al-Hijaz. Planks of wood do not understand or comprehend, and likewise the people of hypocrisy, as if in their neglect of understanding and insight they were in the position of planks of wood.

As for al-musannadah (propped-up): one says "sanada ila shayʾ," meaning he leaned towards something, and "asnadahu ila al-shayʾ," meaning he inclined it, so it is musnad. The doubling (tashdid) is for emphasis. The planks were described with it because they resemble standing trees which grow and bear fruit in some respect. Then He attributed cowardice to them and reproached them for it, saying: ﴿They think every cry is against them.﴾ Muqatil said: when a caller calls out in the army, or an animal escapes, or a lost thing is sought, for example, they think that it is aimed at them because of the terror in their hearts. That is because they are apprehensive lest Allah expose their veils and reveal their secrets, and they expect to be struck moment by moment. Then Allah informed His Messenger of their enmity, saying: ﴿They are the enemy, so beware of them﴾, that you should not trust them with secrets and should not pay attention to their outward appearance, for they are the most complete in enmity relative to others. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿May Allah destroy them! How are they deluded?﴾ is an explanation, and it is an invocation against them, and a request from Him that He curse them and humiliate them, and an instruction to the believers that they should invoke thus. ﴿How are they deluded?﴾ means: how do they turn away from the truth, in wonder at their ignorance, their error, and their corrupt assumption that they are upon the truth.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you"﴾. Al-Kalbi said: when the Qur'an descended upon the Messenger (ﷺ) describing the hypocrites, their tribesmen from among the believers came to them and said: "Woe to you! You have been exposed through hypocrisy and destroyed yourselves. Come to the Messenger of Allah, repent to him from hypocrisy, and ask him to ask forgiveness for you." But they refused that and were indifferent to seeking forgiveness, so this was revealed. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "When ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy returned from Uhud with many people, the Muslims despised him, rebuked him, and made him hear what he disliked. His own kinsmen said to him: 'If you went to the Messenger (ﷺ) so that he would ask forgiveness for you and be pleased with you.' He said: 'I will not go to him, nor do I want him to ask forgiveness for me,' and he began to turn his head, so this was revealed."

According to most, he was only called to seek forgiveness because he had said: ﴿Surely the mightier will expel the meaner therefrom﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8] and said: ﴿Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah﴾. It was said to him: "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you." He said: "What did I say?" That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they turn their heads aside﴾. It was read as lawwaw (without doubling) and with doubling, which is for multiplicity; the pronoun may be treated as plural while the intended referent is singular, and this is common in Arabic poetry. Jarir said:

May Allah not bless those who thought you [would be] ...
except by covenant, until what happened happened.

He addressed this to a woman. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you see them turning away while they are arrogant﴾ means: turning away from the Messenger of Allah's seeking forgiveness (ﷺ). He, exalted is He, mentioned that his seeking forgiveness does not benefit them, so He said: ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them﴾. Qatadah said: this verse was revealed after His saying: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾, because when it was revealed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "My Lord gave me the choice, so I will add to the seventy," and Allah revealed: ﴿Allah will never forgive them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiant people.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: the hypocrites. Some said: in it is a clarification that Allah, exalted is He, possesses a guidance beyond the guidance of explanation, namely the creation of the act of being guided in whomever He knows it of; and it was said: its meaning is that He does not guide them because of their defiance. The Mu'tazilah said: He does not name them guided when they defy and go astray. There are discussions concerning the verse:

The first discussion: why did He liken them to propped-up planks of wood and not to other useful things? We say: this comparison includes many benefits not found in others.

The first: in al-Kashshaf it says: they were likened in their leaning, while they are nothing but bodies empty of faith and goodness, to planks of wood propped against a wall. Also, wood, when it is used, is placed in a roof or wall or other places of use, and as long as it is left empty and not benefited from, it is propped against a wall; so they were likened to it in not being benefited. It may also be meant that the idols carved from wood propped against a wall: they were likened to them in the beauty of their forms and the scarcity of their usefulness.

The second: propped-up planks of wood were originally a fresh branch fit to be among things benefited from, then they become thick and dry; and the unbeliever and hypocrite were likewise originally suitable for such and such, then they leave that suitability.

The third: the disbelievers of mankind are fuel, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell; you are to enter it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98], and propped-up planks are also fuel.

The fourth: one end of propped-up planks is toward one direction and the other end toward another direction, and the hypocrites are likewise, for one end of the hypocrite, which is the inner part, is toward the people of disbelief, and the other end, which is the outer, is toward the people of Islam.

The fifth: what the propped-up planks lean upon is among inanimate things and plants, and what the hypocrites lean upon is likewise; and if they are among the polytheists, it is the idols, which are of inanimate things or plants.

The second discussion: He likened them to propped-up planks of wood, then after that said something that contradicts this comparison, which is

صفحة ١٦
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They think every cry is against them﴾, and planks of wood do not think at all. We say: it is not necessary that the compared and the thing compared to share all attributes. They are like propped-up planks in respect of benefit and non-benefit, but they are not like propped-up planks in respect of hearing or not hearing the cry and other sounds.

The third discussion: He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾, and did not say "the disbelieving people" or "the hypocrites" or "the arrogant," although each of them is among those previously mentioned. We say: each one of those groups is included under His saying "the defiant" (al-fasiqin), that is, those previously mentioned, namely the disbelievers, the hypocrites, and the arrogant.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 63, verses 7–8:

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of God until they disperse." And to God belong the treasuries of the heavens and the earth, but the hypocrites do not understand.﴾ ﴿They say, "If we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it." But to God belongs honor, and to His Messenger and to the believers, but the hypocrites do not know.﴾

God informed of the atrocity of their statement, saying: ﴿They are the ones who say﴾ such and such. "Yanfaddu" means "yatafarraqu" (they disperse). It was also read "yanfadda," from anfada al-qawm, when their provisions ran out. The exegetes said: "The hired man of 'Umar fought with the hired man of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy during one of the expeditions. The hired man of 'Umar made 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy hear what he disliked, and his tongue was harsh against him. 'Abd Allah became angry, and with him was a group of his people. He said: 'By God, if we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it,' meaning by 'the more honorable' himself and by 'the more humble' the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Then he turned to his people and said: 'If you withhold expenditure from these people, meaning the Emigrants, they will soon move away from your homes and lands. So do not spend on them until they disperse from around Muhammad.' Then it was revealed." It was also read "layakhrujanna" with a fatha on the ya'. al-Hasan and Ibn Abi 'Aylah read "lanukhrijanna" with a nun and put al-A'azz and al-Adhall in the accusative.

As for His saying ﴿And to God belong the treasuries of the heavens and the earth﴾, Muqatil said: this means the keys of provision, rain, and vegetation, and the meaning is that God is the Provider: ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?﴾. The people of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: the treasuries of God the Exalted are His decrees, because in them is everything He wills of what He desires to bring forth. al-Junayd said: the treasuries of God the Exalted in the heavens are the unseen matters, and in the earth are the hearts, and He is the Knower of the unseen and the Turner of hearts.

As for His saying ﴿but the hypocrites do not understand﴾, meaning they do not understand that ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82].

As for their saying ﴿If we return﴾, meaning from that expedition, which was the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq, to Medina, God the Exalted answered them and said: ﴿But to God belongs honor﴾, that is, victory and strength, and to whom God honors and supports from His Messenger and from the believers, and honors them by His support of them and by making their religion prevail over all other religions. He informed His Messenger of this. ﴿But the hypocrites do not know this﴾, and had they known it they would not have uttered this statement of theirs.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿But to God belongs honor, and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾, and they are the specific ones for it, just as humiliation and abasement belong to Satan and his followers among the disbelievers and hypocrites.

It is related from one of the righteous women, who was in a shabby state: "Am I not upon Islam, which is the honor that has no humiliation with it, and the wealth that has no poverty with it?"

It is related from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with them both, that a man said to him: "People claim that there is arrogance in you." He said: "It is not arrogance, but it is honor, for this is the honor that has no humiliation with it and the wealth that has no poverty with it," and he recited this verse.

Some of the knowers (al-'arifin), in elucidating this meaning, said: honor (al-'izzah) is not pride (al-kibr), and it is not permissible for the believer to abase himself. Honor is the human being's knowledge of the reality of his own self and his honoring of it, so that he does not place it in lowly, worldly, hasty matters. Pride is the human being's ignorance of himself and his placing of himself above his proper station. Honor resembles pride in form, and differs from it in reality, as humility is confused with lowliness. Humility is praiseworthy, lowliness is blameworthy; pride is blameworthy, and honor is praiseworthy. Since honor is not blameworthy yet has a resemblance to pride, God the Exalted said: ﴿for what you were arrogant about in the earth without right﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 20]. In this there is a subtle indication of the affirmation of honor through truth, and standing at the limit of humility without deviating into lowliness is standing upon the path of honor, laid out over the edge of the fire of pride.

If it is said: In the first verse He said ﴿do not understand﴾ and in the other ﴿do not know﴾, what is the wisdom in this? We say: so that by the first is known their scarcity of shrewdness and understanding, and by the second their great foolishness and ignorance. "La yafqahun" is from faqiha yafqahu, like 'alima ya'lamu, and from faquha yafquhu, like 'azuma ya'zumu. The first is for acquiring understanding through effort, and the second is not through effort. The first is acquired (ʿilajī), the second is innate (mizājī).

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, let not your wealth and your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah. And whoever does that — then it is those who are the losers.﴾ ﴿And spend from what We have provided you before death comes to one of you and he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term so I could give charity and be among the righteous."﴾ ﴿But Allah will never delay a soul when its term has come, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

(لا تُلْهِكم) "let not distract you" — i.e., do not occupy you as they occupied the hypocrites. The exegetes differed: some said it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and others said it was concerning the believers. His saying ﴿from the remembrance of Allah﴾ means from the obligations of Allah the Exalted, such as the prayer, zakat and hajj, or from obedience to Allah the Exalted. Ad-Dahhak said: "the five prayers." According to Muqatil: this verse and what follows is an address to the hypocrites who professed faith. ﴿And whoever does that﴾ means: whoever is diverted by his wealth and his children from the remembrance of Allah. ﴿Then it is those who are the losers﴾ means: in their trade, since they sold the noble and everlasting for the base and perishing. It was also said: they are the losers in denying what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning monotheism and resurrection.

Al-Kalbi said: it means jihad. It was also said: it is the Qur'an, and it was said: it is reflecting upon the Qur'an, contemplating it and pondering over it. ﴿And spend from what We have provided you﴾ — Ibn Abbas said: it means the zakat of wealth, and "min" (from) is for partition. It was also said: what is meant is obligatory spending. ﴿Before death comes to one of you﴾ means: the signs and indications of death. ﴿Then he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me"﴾ — this is his saying: ﴿My Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term.﴾ It was also said: their exhortation is to persevere in remembrance and not to be stingy with wealth, meaning: "Why did You not grant me respite and delay my term until a little time," namely an increase in his term so that he may give charity and purify himself. This is His saying the Exalted: ﴿so I could give charity and be among the righteous.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: this is evidence that those people were not believers, for the believer does not ask to return. Ad-Dahhak said: no one whom death overtakes without having performed the hajj or paid zakat fails to ask to return, and he recited this verse. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "before one sees what leaves him without hope of respite, when the noose tightens around him, when spending becomes impossible for him, and the time of acceptance passes, so that he grieves over his withholding and bites his fingers over the loss of what he had been able to possess." And from Ibn Abbas: "Give charity before there descends upon you the authority of death, for then no repentance is accepted and no deed benefits."

His saying ﴿and be among the righteous﴾ — Ibn Abbas said: "I would perform hajj." It is read as ﴿fa-akūna﴾, and it follows the wording of ﴿fa-aṣṣaddaqa wa-akun﴾. Al-Mubarrad said: "wa-akun" follows what precedes it, because His saying ﴿fa-aṣṣaddaqa﴾ is an answer to the interrogative which contains the wish, and the jussive is upon the position of the fa'. Ubayy read ﴿fa-atasaddaqa﴾ according to the original, and ﴿wa-akun﴾ as a conjunction upon the position of ﴿fa-aṣṣaddaqa﴾. Sibawayh recited many verses in support of applying the rule to the position, among them:

[Mu'awiya, indeed we are human, so be lenient]
fa-lasna bil-jibali wa-la al-hadida
"We are not of mountains, nor of iron,"

where he put "al-hadid" in the accusative as a conjunction upon the position. The "bi" in His saying "bil-jibal" is for emphasis, not for a future meaning that may be omitted or reversed. And the saying of Ibn Abi Sulma:

badā lī annī lastu mudriká mā maḍā ∗∗∗ wa-lā sābiqan shay'an idhā kāna jā'iyā
"It has become clear to me that I cannot overtake what has passed, nor outrun anything when it has come."

He supposed that he said "mudrik" (overtaking) and so he conjoined to it "sabiq," as a conjunction upon the understood meaning. As for the reading of Abu Amr "wa-akūna," he applied it to the wording rather than the meaning.

Then He, the Exalted, informed that He does not delay one whose period has ended and whose term has arrived, so He said: ﴿But Allah will never delay a soul﴾ — meaning, from death when its term has come. The author of al-Kashshaf said: this is a negation of delay in the emphatic manner whose meaning is the impossibility of what is negated. In sum, His saying ﴿Let not your wealth and your children divert you﴾ is an alert to remembrance before death, and ﴿And spend from what We have provided you﴾ is an alert to gratitude for that. His saying the Exalted ﴿and Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ means: even if he were returned to the world, he would neither give zakat nor perform hajj, and this is like His saying: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28]. The exegetes hold that this is an address comprehensive of every deed, whether good or evil. Asim read ﴿ya'malūna﴾ with the "ya" in accordance with His saying ﴿But Allah will never delay a soul﴾, because "nafs" (soul), though singular in form, is intended in a plural sense, so it was construed according to meaning. And Allah knows best; and His blessings and peace be upon our master Muhammad, and his family and all his companions.

"It has become clear to me that I cannot overtake what has passed, nor outrun anything when it has come."

He supposed that he said "mudrik" (overtaking) and so he conjoined to it "sabiq," as a conjunction upon the understood meaning. As for the reading of Abu Amr "wa-akūna," he applied it to the wording rather than the meaning.

Then He, the Exalted, informed that He does not delay one whose period has ended and whose term has arrived, so He said: ﴿But Allah will never delay a soul﴾ — meaning, from death when its term has come. The author of al-Kashshaf said: this is a negation of delay in the emphatic manner whose meaning is the impossibility of what is negated. In sum, His saying ﴿Let not your wealth and your children divert you﴾ is an alert to remembrance before death, and ﴿And spend from what We have provided you﴾ is an alert to gratitude for that. His saying the Exalted ﴿and Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ means: even if he were returned to the world, he would neither give zakat nor perform hajj, and this is like His saying: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28]. The exegetes hold that this is an address comprehensive of every deed, whether good or evil. Asim read ﴿ya'malūna﴾ with the "ya" in accordance with His saying ﴿But Allah will never delay a soul﴾, because "nafs" (soul), though singular in form, is intended in a plural sense, so it was construed according to meaning. And Allah knows best; and His blessings and peace be upon our master Muhammad, and his family and all his companions.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, let not your wealth and your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah. And whoever does that — then it is those who are the losers.﴾ ﴿And spend from what We have provided you before death comes to one of you and he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term so I could give charity and be among the righteous."﴾ ﴿But Allah will never delay a soul when its term has come, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

(لا تُلْهِكم) "let not distract you" — i.e., do not occupy you as they occupied the hypocrites. The exegetes differed: some said it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and others said it was concerning the believers. His saying ﴿from the remembrance of Allah﴾ means from the obligations of Allah the Exalted, such as the prayer, zakat and hajj, or from obedience to Allah the Exalted. Ad-Dahhak said: "the five prayers." According to Muqatil: this verse and what follows is an address to the hypocrites who professed faith. ﴿And whoever does that﴾ means: whoever is diverted by his wealth and his children from the remembrance of Allah. ﴿Then it is those who are the losers﴾ means: in their trade, since they sold the noble and everlasting for the base and perishing. It was also said: they are the losers in denying what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning monotheism and resurrection.

Al-Kalbi said: it means jihad. It was also said: it is the Qur'an, and it was said: it is reflecting upon the Qur'an, contemplating it and pondering over it. ﴿And spend from what We have provided you﴾ — Ibn Abbas said: it means the zakat of wealth, and "min" (from) is for partition. It was also said: what is meant is obligatory spending. ﴿Before death comes to one of you﴾ means: the signs and indications of death. ﴿Then he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me"﴾ — this is his saying: ﴿My Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term.﴾ It was also said: their exhortation is to persevere in remembrance and not to be stingy with wealth, meaning: "Why did You not grant me respite and delay my term until a little time," namely an increase in his term so that he may give charity and purify himself. This is His saying the Exalted: ﴿so I could give charity and be among the righteous.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: this is evidence that those people were not believers, for the believer does not ask to return. Ad-Dahhak said: no one whom death overtakes without having performed the hajj or paid zakat fails to ask to return, and he recited this verse. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "before one sees what leaves him without hope of respite, when the noose tightens around him, when spending becomes impossible for him, and the time of acceptance passes, so that he grieves over his withholding and bites his fingers over the loss of what he had been able to possess." And from Ibn Abbas: "Give charity before there descends upon you the authority of death, for then no repentance is accepted and no deed benefits."

His saying ﴿and be among the righteous﴾ — Ibn Abbas said: "I would perform hajj." It is read as ﴿fa-akūna﴾, and it follows the wording of ﴿fa-aṣṣaddaqa wa-akun﴾. Al-Mubarrad said: "wa-akun" follows what precedes it, because His saying ﴿fa-aṣṣaddaqa﴾ is an answer to the interrogative which contains the wish, and the jussive is upon the position of the fa'. Ubayy read ﴿fa-atasaddaqa﴾ according to the original, and ﴿wa-akun﴾ as a conjunction upon the position of ﴿fa-aṣṣaddaqa﴾. Sibawayh recited many verses in support of applying the rule to the position, among them:

[Mu'awiya, indeed we are human, so be lenient]
fa-lasna bil-jibali wa-la al-hadida
"We are not of mountains, nor of iron,"

where he put "al-hadid" in the accusative as a conjunction upon the position. The "bi" in His saying "bil-jibal" is for emphasis, not for a future meaning that may be omitted or reversed. And the saying of Ibn Abi Sulma:
